title: Coral and the Undertow
premise: Wren Reyes, a celebrated restaurant critic who lost his sense of taste after his mother's death, drifts through Manila's dining scene writing reviews he cannot feel. When he is sent to profile Magdalena 'Lola Inday' Villaruel, the last fluent speaker of a dying coastal language, she refuses to be interviewed—instead demanding he become her final student. As Wren learns words for tide, salt, and grief in a tongue no one else will carry, he uncovers the story of the fishing village she lost and confronts the tasteless silence he built around his own loss. When Lola Inday's health fails, Wren must record, translate, and finally speak her language aloud at her bedside and then at her wake, discovering that mourning out loud restores what survival had cost him: by the last chapter, tasting a simple bowl of her sinigang recipe, he weeps—and belongs.
about_author: Lior Brightwater is the pen name of a former food writer turned novelist who spent two years documenting endangered Philippine languages before writing fiction. They live between coastal towns and city kitchens, collecting recipes they refuse to simplify.

chapters.title: The Tenant
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. A day in his numb life: reviewing an acclaimed tasting menu he cannot taste, filing copy on instinct alone, eating alone in a spotless apartment that feels rented rather than owned. Flashbacks hint at his mother's death three years ago. Emotional beat: hollow competence masking grief.

chapters.title: Assignment
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. His editor assigns a human-interest feature on Lola Inday, the last speaker of Binukid-ni-Dagat, a coastal language down to one voice. Wren protests—he writes about food, not people—but the editor insists the story is really about a cuisine dying with its language. Beat: reluctant first step outward.

chapters.title: The House Above the Waterline
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. He travels to the shrinking fishing village of Balisong Cove and meets Lola Inday, sharp-tongued and unimpressed by his credentials. She feeds him a bowl of soup and asks what it tastes like; he lies; she knows. She refuses the interview. Beat: being seen through for the first time in years.

chapters.title: Salt Words
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Returning with his recorder, Lola Inday offers a counterproposal: no interview until he learns one hundred words of her language. The first lessons are names for water, wind, and fish—words with no English equivalents. Beat: curiosity cracking open his armor.

chapters.title: A Hundred Tides
chapters.summary: Wren's POV, interwoven with Lola Inday's spoken memories. He begins commuting to the cove weekly; the village children adopt him as 'the student.' He learns the word for 'the smell of rain arriving over sea.' Beat: tentative belonging, unfamiliar warmth.

chapters.title: What the Mother Left
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. A flashback chapter: his mother's kitchen, her death, the meal he cooked from her recipe card that tasted of nothing—the moment his palate broke. Present-day Wren realizes Lola Inday's lessons keep circling the same wound. Beat: grief named at last.

chapters.title: The Village That Spoke
chapters.summary: Lola Inday's POV (rendered as her dictated testimony). The cove forty years ago: a community singing work songs in Binukid-ni-Dagat, the typhoon, the relocation, the slow switch to Tagalog and English for survival. Beat: elegy; the price of survival made concrete.

chapters.title: Mistranslation
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. At a lavish awards dinner, Wren freezes mid-speech when asked to describe flavor, and publicly stumbles. A rival critic smells weakness. Back home he finds himself practicing vocabulary instead of sleeping. Beat: his double life splitting him open.

chapters.title: Word Forty-Nine
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Lesson sessions deepen; Lola Inday teaches him lullabies and insults, laughter and curses. Word forty-nine is 'to grieve someone while they still live.' Wren recognizes it instantly. First real argument between them about whether remembering is enough. Beat: intimacy through friction.

chapters.title: The Rival Review
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. A scathing profile of Wren appears, questioning whether the famous critic ever tasted anything at all. His editor demands damage control; Wren, oddly relieved to be exposed, goes quiet. He misses a lesson for the first time. Beat: professional identity collapsing.

chapters.title: Net Mending
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. He returns to the cove ashamed; instead of scolding, Lola Inday puts him to work mending nets with the fishermen, hands busy, words optional. The village quietly folds him into its rhythms—a borrowed chair, a standing invitation. Beat: found family forming without ceremony.

chapters.title: The Recipe Book
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Lola Inday reveals a water-stained notebook of recipes written in her language, each dish tied to a song and a dead relative. She wants it translated before she dies—but only if Wren can cook them, not just read them. Beat: stakes sharpen into a mission.

chapters.title: First Dish
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. In the cove's communal kitchen, Wren attempts kinilaw under the supervision of laughing aunties. It is wrong—too sour, no memory in it—but everyone eats it anyway. He tastes nothing, yet something loosens. Beat: failure embraced as participation.

chapters.title: The Fall
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Lola Inday suffers a stroke; hospital corridors replace the porch lessons. Wren keeps vigil beside her estranged grandnephew Jun, who resents the old woman's stubbornness. The recording device sits unused. Beat: fear; time announced as an enemy.

chapters.title: Seventy-One Words Remaining
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. In the hospital, Lola Inday, speech slurred but will intact, resumes lessons from her bed. Nurses become accidental students. Wren records everything, terrified the archive will be all that survives. Beat: urgency transformed into devotion.

chapters.title: Jun
chapters.summary: Jun's POV. The grandnephew's chapter: his resentment, his childhood summers in the cove, the words he refused to learn out of teenage shame. Watching Wren—a stranger—carry what he abandoned, Jun begins sitting in on lessons. Beat: guilt turning toward repair.

chapters.title: The Feast That Was Promised
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Lola Inday's dying wish: one feast cooked entirely from the notebook, eaten aloud in her language, so the dishes 'go somewhere' instead of ending with her. Wren and Jun plan it; the village commits. Beat: hope braided with dread.

chapters.title: Undertow
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Two days before the feast, Lola Inday declines sharply. Wren panics—his old pattern, wanting to disappear before losing again—and nearly flees to the city. On the bus he tastes salt on his lips and turns back. Beat: darkest hour; the choice to stay.

chapters.title: The Last Speaker Speaks
chapters.summary: Lola Inday's POV. Her final lucid evening: she tells Wren the story she withheld—the daughter lost to the typhoon, the reason she stopped teaching anyone. She makes Wren promise not to archive the language but to speak it, badly, daily, out loud. Beat: confession and charge.

chapters.title: Feast of Names
chapters.summary: Ensemble POV. The feast: long tables above the waterline, every dish from the notebook, every toast in Binukid-ni-Dagat, Wren's accent broken but unashamed. Lola Inday attends in a wheelchair, naming each ancestor as each dish lands. Beat: climax; communal resurrection.

chapters.title: Goodbye, Out Loud
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Lola Inday dies at dawn nine days later. At the wake, Wren delivers the eulogy in her language, then translates it into English so the whole village weeps twice. Jun announces he will continue the lessons. Beat: grief performed properly, at last.

chapters.title: Taste
chapters.summary: Wren's POV, epilogue. Months later: Wren has resigned from criticism, teaches Saturday classes in the cove, and cooks his mother's sinigang from her card. He takes one spoonful—and tastes it: sour, salt, sweet, sorrow. He writes one final review, five hundred words about a single bowl. Beat: resolution; belonging earned, survival redefined.
